extra.message: Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads on request body — Remote code execution on the server by sending a malicious pickle payload. [verified: pickle.loads is called on raw request body/GET-controlled bytes with no allowlist or signature check, giving RCE gated only by the weak static token.]

Server-side template injection via fragment parameter — Arbitrary code execution via Jinja2 SSTI payloads (e.g. accessing __class__.__mro__ or os module through gadget chains). [verified: fragment GET param is string-concatenated into Jinja2 Template source and rendered with no sandboxing, enabling SSTI/RCE.]

Server-side template injection via Jinja2 Template.render — Remote code execution through Jinja2 sandbox escape / global namespace access [verified: Duplicate of finding 3 — same unsandboxed Jinja2 Template.render() on concatenated user input confirming SSTI/RCE.]

OS command injection via host parameter — Arbitrary OS command execution on the server as the application user. [verified: request.GET.get('host') is concatenated directly into an os.system shell string with no sanitization, allowing shell metacharacter injection.]

Hardcoded default Django SECRET_KEY — Attacker who knows the default key can forge signed session cookies, CSRF tokens, and password-reset tokens, leading to full account takeover. [verified: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded, publicly-known string shipped in .env.example, enabling forged sessions/CSRF/password-reset tokens if operator doesn't override it.]

Sensitive operational endpoints gated only by static shared token — A single leaked/guessed static token grants access to command execution, deserialization, and arbitrary file write across the whole module [verified: _wrk_gate uses a plain '==' comparison (timing side-channel) and is the sole control gating destructive operations (pickle, os.system, arbitrary file write) across the whole module, matching the threat model's weaker-trust-boundary concern.]

Path traversal via ref parameter and sensitive data written via GET — Arbitrary file write outside intended export directory, plus PII/simulated card data exposure via URL/query string and logs. [verified: 'ref' param is used unsanitized in a file path under BASE_EXPORT_DIR, and PII/simulated SSN/card values from GET are persisted to disk/logs.]

Unauthenticated partner_console endpoint — Attacker can invoke this internal ops endpoint without any credential, bypassing the intended static-token gate used everywhere else in the module. [verified: acct_identity_ping_337 (line 106) never calls _wrk_gate, unlike every sibling handler, so it is reachable with no auth at all.]

Reflected CORS origin with credentials allowed — Any malicious website can make credentialed requests to this endpoint and read the response, enabling cross-origin data theft. [verified: Origin header is reflected verbatim into Access-Control-Allow-Origin alongside Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, the classic credentialed-CORS-reflection flaw.]

Credentialed CORS reflects arbitrary Origin — Any malicious website can make credentialed cross-origin requests and read responses from this endpoint [verified: Duplicate of finding 6 — same Origin reflection plus Allow-Credentials: true credentialed CORS misconfiguration.]

Path traversal / arbitrary file write via name parameter — Attacker can write arbitrary files anywhere writable on the filesystem, potentially overwriting application code or planting a webshell. [verified: 'name' GET param is joined directly into BASE_EXPORT_DIR with no path sanitization and the request body is written there, allowing traversal outside the intended directory.]

Debug mode enabled by default — Unauthenticated attackers triggering any server error see full Django debug tracebacks including source code, local variable values, request data, and settings, aiding further exploitation. [verified: DEBUG defaults to true via getenv fallback matching .env.example shipped default, exposing full debug tracebacks to unauthenticated users on any unhandled exception.]

Cross-tenant account takeover via contact_invite — An Account Manager in one tenant can silently reassign another tenant's user account into their own organization and change its role, and (if the target account was previously unset) can also gain a known static password to log in as that user. [verified: get_or_create keys on username=contact.email with no check that an existing user belongs to another org, and update_or_create unconditionally rewrites that user's Profile role/organization; can_manage_org only checks the acting user's own org membership, not the target user's prior identity.]

Sensitive data (Authorization header, raw body) written to logs — Credentials/tokens and potentially sensitive payload contents persist in log files, exposing them to anyone with log access. [verified: logger.warning logs the full raw request body and Authorization header unredacted at line 42.]

Open redirect via lane parameter — Attacker can craft links that redirect victims from a trusted domain to an arbitrary malicious site, aiding phishing. [verified: redirect() targets the raw 'lane' GET param with no same-site/allowlist validation, enabling open redirect.]

Unvalidated ledger state/amount manipulation — Attacker (with the static ops token) can force any ledger record into an 'approved' state or manipulate balance arbitrarily, bypassing intended approval workflow/business rules [verified: 'amount' and 'state' are taken directly from attacker-controlled payload/query and used to mutate ledger balance/state with no validation or business-rule enforcement.]

Mass assignment of privileged fields (role/approved) — Attacker can escalate role/approval state fields that should be server-controlled [verified: workset.update(payload) merges the entire attacker-controlled JSON directly into a dict containing 'role'/'approved' with no field allowlist, then returns it.]

Predictable PRNG used to generate security code — Attacker can predict or brute-force generated codes, e.g. bypassing verification flows [verified: Duplicate of finding 11 — non-CSPRNG random module used for a security code.]

Privilege escalation via client-controlled cookie — Attacker sets ops_badge=lead cookie/header to unlock elevated response data without any real authorization. [verified: An unauthenticated-context cookie/header value (ops_badge) alone grants an elevated data lane with no identity-tied server-side authorization check.]

Disabled TLS certificate verification on outbound request — Susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks on outbound traffic; attacker-controlled network path could intercept/modify responses. [verified: ssl._create_unverified_context() is used for the outbound HTTPS call, disabling certificate validation.]

Missing secure cookie / transport-security settings — Session and CSRF cookies can be sent over unencrypted HTTP and captured via network MITM, leading to session hijacking. [verified: No SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE/CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE/SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT/HSTS settings are present, leaving Django's insecure HTTP-transmittable cookie defaults in effect.]

Hardcoded static password for invited customer contacts — Account takeover of any newly-invited customer_contact account using a publicly known fixed password, since it is never forced to be changed. [verified: A static hardcoded password 'DemoPass123!' is set for every newly created invited user with no forced reset or expiry, and it is echoed in the UI, making any newly-invited contact account guessable/known.]

Mass assignment of Contact.permissions via CSV import — Account Manager can grant a customer contact elevated 'admin' contact-permissions by crafting the imported CSV, bypassing normal contact-creation controls. [verified: The 'permissions' CSV column is passed directly into Contact.objects.update_or_create defaults with only Django field-choice validation, no application-level whitelist, letting an Account Manager set permissions='admin' via crafted CSV.]

Weak unsalted MD5 hash used for sensitive value — Trivial to reverse via rainbow tables/brute force, undermining any integrity/secrecy guarantee the digest was meant to provide. [verified: Unsalted MD5 is used to digest a security-relevant 'phrase' value, which is fast to brute-force.]

Weak unsalted MD5 hash for sensitive phrase — Trivial offline brute-force/rainbow-table recovery of the original secret phrase [verified: Duplicate of finding 10 — unsalted MD5 on a sensitive phrase value.]

Account/handle enumeration via distinct error responses — Attacker with the static ops token can enumerate valid internal handle names, aiding further targeted attacks (e.g. brute-forcing the 4-digit verifier for a confirmed-valid handle) [verified: Distinct 404 vs 403 responses for unknown handle vs bad verifier (lines 118 and 120) let a caller enumerate valid handles.]

Brute-forceable verifier code with no rate limiting — Attacker can brute-force the short numeric verifier to pass the identity check and reach the protected 'queued' response, defeating the verification control [verified: 4-digit numeric verifier checked against a tiny fixed keyspace with no lockout/rate-limiting, trivially brute-forceable.]

Security headers disabled (CSP/X-XSS-Protection) — Removes defense-in-depth browser protections, increasing impact of any XSS elsewhere reflected through this response path. [verified: X-XSS-Protection is explicitly set to 0 and CSP is emptied, removing browser-side mitigations on that response path.]

CSV formula injection in export_csv — Attacker-controlled formula injection executed in the spreadsheet application of any admin who opens an exported report, potentially leading to code execution or data exfiltration on that admin's machine. [verified: export_csv writes org.name/deal.name/esc.title (all user-editable via forms) via csv.writer.writerow with no leading =/+/-/@ neutralization, enabling formula injection when opened in Excel/Sheets by an admin.]
